patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.setting: GP surgery, then the Emergency Department
patient.complaint: Getting up four times a night to pass urine, with a weak stream
background: No falls; lives with his wife

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older man, nocturia and a weak stream: the DRE (smooth vs hard and irregular) and the PSA separate BPH from prostate cancer.

points: Desmond, 68, gets up **four times a night** to pass urine.
Stream is **weak** and stops and starts.
He waits to get going (**hesitancy**) and dribbles afterwards.
Feels the bladder never fully empties.
No weight loss, no blood in the urine, no bone pain.

steps.lead: Desmond has the full house of voiding **LUTS** plus nocturia. The DRE and PSA are the next two clues the exam gives you.
At 68 he is well inside the **over-50** group, and DHT has been driving his gland for decades.

points: DRE: **smooth, firm, symmetrically enlarged** prostate.
Central (median) sulcus is **preserved**.
No hard nodules; not tender.
Abdomen soft; bladder not palpable today.

steps.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
steps.r: Voiding LUTS with a **smooth, enlarged, firm** prostate in an older man is BPH. Cancer is hard and irregular; prostatitis is tender.

steps.lead: Desmond's gland is growing in the **transition zone**, which wraps around the urethra. That is why his stream is weak.
If Desmond had been left untreated for longer, the classic exam sign would be this **painless, smooth suprapubic mass**.

visual.title: Where the mass is in chronic retention
visual.caption: A firm, smooth, **painless** suprapubic mass that is dull to percussion: a chronically distended bladder.

steps.text: Painless = chronic retention. Painful with inability to void = acute retention.

steps.lead: Desmond needs to know the risks of leaving it: retention, infection, stones and kidney damage.

steps.text: Anticholinergic drugs (**cyclizine**, oxybutynin, tricyclics) can tip a man with BPH into **acute urinary retention**. Check the drug chart when an older man suddenly cannot void.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (urine dipstick), questions on when PSA can be measured, and 'Which investigation assesses outflow obstruction?' (bladder ultrasound and uroflowmetry).

steps.q: What is the first test to do in the surgery today?
steps.r: A **urine dipstick** rules out infection, which can cause or worsen LUTS. It is quick, cheap and done first.

steps.lead: Desmond has a dipstick, a DRE, and a counselled PSA. He cycled to the surgery, so PSA waits **48 hours**.

steps.title: Desmond's results
steps.text: No infection, a PSA in range and normal kidneys: this fits BPH.
PSA rules: no ejaculation or vigorous exercise for **48 hours**, and wait **6 weeks** after a UTI, prostatitis or biopsy, or it will be falsely high.

steps.lead: To see how badly Desmond's bladder empties, a **post-void residual** on bladder ultrasound and a flow rate are the next tests.

points: Uroflowmetry: low peak flow with a long, flat curve.
Bladder scan after voiding: **160 mL** left behind.
Kidneys on ultrasound: no hydronephrosis.

steps.lead: Desmond fills in the **IPSS** questionnaire: frequency, nocturia, urgency, weak stream, straining and incomplete emptying.

visual.title: IPSS (International Prostate Symptom Score)
visual.label: Desmond 18
visual.caption: Above 7 means moderate to severe symptoms: drug treatment, not just lifestyle advice.

steps.text: Do not jump to **MRI prostate or biopsy** with a smooth gland and a normal PSA. Those are for suspected cancer.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (tamsulosin if IPSS >7), the next step when the gland is big or tamsulosin is unsuitable (finasteride), and catheterisation for acute retention.

points: IPSS 18; Desmond is fed up with broken sleep.
No history of falls or dizziness on standing.
He does not want an operation.

steps.q: Which is the best first treatment for Desmond?
steps.r: IPSS above 7 means drug treatment, and the first-line drug is an **alpha-1 antagonist** such as tamsulosin.

steps.lead: Desmond's IPSS of 18 puts him past lifestyle advice alone. He also cuts his evening tea and stops fluids before bed.

steps.text: Tamsulosin causes **postural hypotension**. If the stem mentions falls or dizziness on standing, the answer is usually not an alpha-blocker.

points: Six months on: better stream, still up twice a night.
Transrectal ultrasound estimate: prostate about **55 g**.
Still no urgency or urge incontinence.

steps.lead: Desmond's gland is well over **30 g**, so a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor is added to his tamsulosin.

visual.title: Prostate volume after adding finasteride
visual.caption: Finasteride shrinks the gland slowly: it takes about **6 months** to work.

steps.title: BPH treatment ladder
nodes: IPSS ≤7: lifestyle (less caffeine, alcohol, evening fluid)
Big gland (>30 g) or alpha-blocker unsuitable: finasteride

steps.lead: The IPSS is the rung-finder: Desmond's score decides whether he gets advice alone or drugs.
If Desmond's symptoms stay severe despite both drugs, he would be offered **TURP**.

steps.text: The most common complication after TURP is **retrograde ejaculation**. Warn every man before surgery.

points: A year later: gastroenteritis, given **cyclizine** for vomiting.
Next day: cannot pass urine for 10 hours, lower abdominal agony.
Tender, distended bladder up to the umbilicus.

steps.r: Acute urinary retention needs the bladder drained **now** with a catheter. Everything else comes after.

steps.lead: Desmond's painful, palpable bladder after cyclizine is **acute urinary retention**: catheterise immediately and stop the culprit drug.

science.exam: Science questions ask how finasteride and tamsulosin work, why the transition zone causes obstruction, and why PSA can be mildly raised.

steps.lead: Desmond's gland grows around the urethra because the **transition zone** is the part that hyperplases.

steps.title: How DHT grows the prostate
steps.caption: Finasteride blocks the second box, so less DHT and a smaller gland.

steps.lead: Tamsulosin helped Desmond within days because it relaxes smooth muscle, but his gland stayed the same size.

steps.title: Tamsulosin or finasteride?
head: Tamsulosin
Finasteride
rows: Relaxes prostate and bladder neck muscle

steps.q: Why did Desmond's PSA sit at 2.6 rather than zero?
o: More glandular tissue makes more PSA
steps.r: PSA comes from prostatic epithelium, so a bigger gland makes more. In BPH it is normal or only **mildly** raised.

steps.lead: A mildly raised PSA in BPH has to be told apart from the **markedly** raised PSA of prostate cancer.
Left untreated, Desmond's bladder would work harder against the obstruction, then fail.

mcq.q: Which zone of the prostate is most commonly affected in BPH?
mcq.r: BPH arises in the **transition zone** around the urethra; cancer favours the peripheral zone.

mcq.q: Which finding on DRE fits BPH?
mcq.r: BPH: **smooth, enlarged, firm**. Hard and irregular with a lost sulcus suggests cancer.

mcq.q: Which drug commonly precipitates acute urinary retention in BPH?
mcq.r: **Cyclizine** is anticholinergic and weakens detrusor contraction.

mcq.q: What is the first-line test in a man with LUTS?
How long after a UTI should PSA testing be delayed?
mcq.r: Wait **6 weeks** after UTI, prostatitis or biopsy; 48 hours after ejaculation or exercise.

mcq.q: Which tool scores LUTS severity in BPH?
What is first-line drug treatment for BPH with IPSS above 7?
How long does finasteride take to work?
mcq.r: It shrinks the gland slowly, over about **6 months**.

mcq.q: What is the definitive treatment for severe refractory BPH?
Which hormone drives prostatic growth in BPH?

technique.stem: A 64 year old man has a 1 year history of getting up three times a night to pass urine. His stream is poor and he has to wait before it starts. He has no weight loss or bone pain. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, firm, enlarged prostate with a preserved median sulcus. His PSA is 2.2 µg/L (<4).
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question in an older man with urinary symptoms: decide benign vs malignant vs infective.
Nocturia, weak stream and hesitancy are voiding LUTS. A smooth gland with a kept sulcus and normal PSA is benign.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Voiding LUTS + smooth enlarged prostate + normal PSA = **BPH**.

elim: Prostatitis is painful, febrile and the gland is very tender.
Overactive bladder gives urgency and frequency, not a weak stream and an enlarged gland.
Cancer gives a hard, irregular gland with a lost sulcus and a high PSA.
Stricture affects younger men after infection or instrumentation, with a normal prostate.

steps.x: **B. Benign prostatic hyperplasia.** Rule: smooth = benign, hard and irregular = cancer, tender = prostatitis.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has nocturia, a weak stream and a feeling of incomplete emptying. His urine dipstick is negative. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, enlarged prostate. His PSA is 3.1 µg/L (<4). His GP wants to know how much urine is left in the bladder after voiding.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?

steps.x: An investigation question that tells you exactly what the GP wants: how much urine stays behind.

clues: how much urine is left in the bladder after voiding
steps.x: Infection already excluded, benign-feeling gland. The question is a **post-void residual**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Post-void residual = **bladder ultrasound** (with uroflowmetry for flow).

elim: An X-ray shows stones, not how much urine is left behind.
Cystoscopy looks for bladder tumours (e.g. haematuria), not emptying.
MRI prostate is for suspected cancer; this gland is smooth with a normal PSA.
Biopsy is for a PI-RADS ≥3 lesion, not benign LUTS.

steps.x: **B. Bladder ultrasound.** Rule: dipstick first, then bladder scan and flow rate for outflow obstruction.

technique.stem: A 69 year old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia has taken tamsulosin for 6 months. His stream has improved a little but he still has troublesome nocturia and hesitancy. He has no urgency. His IPSS is 21. Transrectal ultrasound estimates the prostate at 70 g. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

steps.x: Next step in management: he is already on the first rung, so climb the ladder.
Partial response to an alpha-blocker, a very large gland, no storage symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Big gland on tamsulosin: add a **5-alpha-reductase inhibitor** (combination therapy).

elim: An antimuscarinic is added for persisting **storage** symptoms (urgency); he has none.
Radical prostatectomy is a cancer operation, not BPH treatment.
His IPSS is 21: symptoms are severe, so stepping down is wrong.
Alfuzosin is another alpha-blocker; it will not shrink a 70 g gland.

steps.x: **A. Add finasteride.** Rule: gland >30 g = finasteride; urgency persists = antimuscarinic; refractory = TURP.

technique.stem: A 66 year old man with lower urinary tract symptoms starts tamsulosin. Two weeks later his stream is much stronger. A repeat ultrasound at 3 months shows the prostate is the same size as before treatment.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the improvement?
o: Blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT
Relaxes smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck

steps.x: A mechanism question: match the speed of response and the unchanged gland size to the drug action.
Fast benefit with no change in size points to muscle relaxation, not shrinkage.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Tamsulosin blocks **alpha-1 receptors** in prostatic smooth muscle and bladder neck, so they relax.

elim: That is finasteride, which shrinks the gland over months.
Tamsulosin does not act on the detrusor's contraction.
The scan shows the gland has not shrunk.
Tamsulosin is not a diuretic or antidiuretic.

steps.x: **E. Relaxes smooth muscle.** Rule: alpha-blocker = fast, no shrinkage; finasteride = slow, shrinks.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man has an 18 month history of a poor urinary stream, hesitancy and terminal dribbling. He gets up twice a night to pass urine. He has no haematuria or weight loss. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, non-tender prostate. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Voiding LUTS with a smooth, symmetrically enlarged, non-tender prostate is BPH. Prostate cancer would feel hard and irregular.

steps.x: Most likely diagnosis in an older man with LUTS: let the DRE decide.

clues: poor urinary stream, hesitancy and terminal dribbling
steps.x: Voiding LUTS with a smooth, symmetric, non-tender prostate and no red flags.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Prostatitis causes fever, perineal pain and a very tender gland.
Bladder cancer presents with painless visible haematuria.
Cancer gives a hard, asymmetric, irregular gland.
A stricture gives a weak stream but a normal prostate, often after instrumentation.

steps.x: **B. Benign prostatic hyperplasia.** Smooth and symmetric = benign.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has nocturia, hesitancy and a weak stream for 2 years. He is otherwise well with no bone pain. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 134/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on digital rectal examination?
o: Hard, irregular prostate with loss of the median sulcus
Rectal mass separate from the prostate
practice.e: BPH feels smooth, firm and enlarged. A hard, irregular gland with a lost sulcus is the cancer distractor.

steps.x: A 'most likely finding' question: predict the examination from the story.

clues: nocturia, hesitancy and a weak stream for 2 years
steps.x: Long-standing voiding LUTS in an older man with no red flags is BPH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BPH on DRE: **smooth, firm, enlarged**, sulcus kept.

elim: That is acute prostatitis, with fever and pain.
That is the cancer pattern; there are no red flags and LUTS fit BPH.
Voiding LUTS for 2 years in a 72 year old implies an enlarged gland.
A rectal mass suggests colorectal cancer, not his urinary picture.

steps.x: **E. Smooth, firm, enlarged prostate.**

practice.stem: A 79 year old man has dribbling incontinence and passes small volumes of urine frequently. He has had a weak stream for years. There is a firm, smooth, non-tender swelling arising from the pelvis that is dull to percussion. The rest of the abdomen is soft. His pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 150/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A painless, smooth, dull suprapubic mass with overflow dribbling is chronic retention from BPH. Acute retention is painful.

steps.x: Diagnosis: a painless suprapubic mass in an older man with long-standing LUTS.
Overflow dribbling plus a painless, dull suprapubic mass is a chronically full bladder from BPH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic urinary retention** due to BPH.

elim: Acute retention is painful with complete inability to void.
A bladder tumour presents with haematuria, not a smooth painless distended bladder.
Overactive bladder does not produce a palpable distended bladder.
UTI causes dysuria and frequency, not a painless pelvic mass.

steps.x: **C. Chronic urinary retention.** Rule: painless = chronic, painful = acute.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia on tamsulosin is admitted with vomiting from gastroenteritis. He is given an antiemetic. Twelve hours later he has severe lower abdominal pain and cannot pass urine. His bladder is palpable and tender. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 164/92 mmHg.
practice.q: Which drug is the most likely cause?
practice.e: Cyclizine is anticholinergic and precipitates acute urinary retention in BPH. Ondansetron and domperidone do not.

steps.x: Cause question: which drug tips a man with BPH into acute retention?
BPH plus a new antiemetic plus painful inability to void = drug-induced acute retention.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The anticholinergic antiemetic: **cyclizine**.

elim: Amoxicillin does not affect bladder emptying.
Domperidone is a dopamine antagonist without anticholinergic effect on the bladder.
A PPI does not cause urinary retention.
Ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) causes constipation, not retention.

steps.x: **B. Cyclizine.** Anticholinergics weaken the detrusor against a fixed obstruction.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has untreated lower urinary tract symptoms for 5 years and two urinary tract infections this year. His prostate is smooth and enlarged. Ultrasound shows bilateral hydronephrosis and a thick-walled bladder with a large post-void residual. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 146/88 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his renal impairment?
practice.e: Chronic BPH obstruction causes detrusor hypertrophy, residual urine, recurrent UTI and bilateral hydronephrosis. Unilateral ureteric causes would not thicken the bladder.

steps.x: Cause question: link the scan to the long history.

clues: untreated lower urinary tract symptoms for 5 years
steps.x: Years of obstruction led to detrusor hypertrophy, residual urine, infection and back-pressure on both kidneys.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bladder outlet obstruction** from BPH.

elim: There is no NSAID history, and it does not cause hydronephrosis or a big residual.
His glucose is normal and diabetic nephropathy does not cause hydronephrosis.
RAS gives small kidneys and hypertension, not a dilated collecting system.
That obstructs the ureters, but the bladder would not be thick-walled with a big residual.

steps.x: **B. Bladder outlet obstruction.** Bilateral hydronephrosis + big residual = obstruction below the bladder.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has woken four times a night to pass urine for a year. His stream is weak and he strains to void. He is not thirsty and has no ankle swelling. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, enlarged prostate.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his nocturia?
practice.e: Nocturia with a weak stream, straining and a smooth enlarged prostate, with normal glucose and sodium, is BPH.

steps.x: Cause of nocturia: rule out the metabolic and cardiac causes first.
Voiding symptoms and an enlarged gland, with no thirst, high sugar or oedema.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: BPH, the **most common cause of nocturia** in older men.

elim: DI gives polyuria and thirst with a low urine osmolality.
His glucose is normal and he is not thirsty.
Heart failure nocturia comes with oedema and breathlessness; he has neither.
Overactive bladder causes urgency, not a weak stream and straining.

steps.x: **A. Benign prostatic hyperplasia.**

practice.stem: A 63 year old man has a 6 month history of hesitancy, frequency and a weak stream. He has no fever or dysuria. Abdominal examination is normal. His GP is starting the work-up today.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: A urine dipstick is the first test in LUTS to exclude infection. Uroflowmetry and bladder ultrasound come second.

steps.x: Initial investigation: the cheapest, first test in LUTS.

clues: hesitancy, frequency and a weak stream
steps.x: LUTS work-up starts by excluding infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urine dipstick.**

elim: CT KUB is for stones, not routine LUTS.
Cystoscopy is for haematuria or suspected bladder cancer.
Biopsy needs MRI findings first and is for cancer.
Flow studies are second-line, after infection has been ruled out.

steps.x: **D. Urine dipstick.** Then DRE and counselled PSA, then bladder scan and flow.

practice.stem: A 67 year old man with lower urinary tract symptoms asks for a PSA test. He was treated for a urinary tract infection 2 weeks ago and is now well. His prostate feels smooth and enlarged. His temperature is 36.5°C, pulse rate 68 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
practice.q: When is the most appropriate time to measure his PSA?
practice.e: PSA should be delayed 6 weeks after a UTI, prostatitis or biopsy. The 48 hour rule applies to ejaculation and exercise.

steps.x: A timing question about PSA: find what has recently happened to his prostate.
A UTI inflames the prostate and raises PSA for weeks.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Wait **6 weeks** after a UTI.

elim: 48 hours is the rule after ejaculation or vigorous exercise, not after a UTI.
There is no need to wait that long.
The recent UTI may still be raising his PSA falsely.
A counselled PSA is appropriate in LUTS now; haematuria is not the trigger.

steps.x: **A. 6 weeks after the infection.** 48 hours for ejaculation or exercise; 6 weeks for UTI, prostatitis or biopsy.

practice.stem: A 65 year old man has nocturia, hesitancy and a weak stream. His IPSS is 15. He has no history of falls or dizziness. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, enlarged prostate, estimated at 25 g. His PSA is 1.8 µg/L (<4). His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 140/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: IPSS above 7 with no contraindication means an alpha-1 antagonist first. Finasteride is for big glands or when tamsulosin is unsuitable.

steps.x: Initial management: use the IPSS to find the rung.

clues: no history of falls or dizziness
steps.x: Moderate symptoms, small gland, no reason to avoid an alpha-blocker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Tamsulosin** (alpha-1 antagonist).

elim: Finasteride is for a gland over 30 g or when an alpha-blocker is unsuitable.
Lifestyle alone is for mild symptoms (IPSS ≤7).
An antimuscarinic is for storage symptoms, and may cause retention here.
TURP is for severe, refractory disease.

steps.x: **D. Tamsulosin.** IPSS >7 = alpha-blocker first.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man has moderate lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia. He has had three falls this year and his BP drops on standing. Ultrasound estimates the prostate at 60 g. His pulse rate is 76 bpm, BP 138/80 mmHg lying and 112/68 mmHg standing.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Alpha-blockers are contraindicated with falls and orthostatic hypotension, and his gland is over 30 g, so finasteride is used.

steps.x: Management with a twist: what stops you using the usual first-line drug?
Falls and orthostatic hypotension contraindicate alpha-blockers; the gland is well over 30 g.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **5-alpha-reductase inhibitor**: finasteride.

elim: Alfuzosin is also an alpha-blocker and will worsen postural hypotension.
Doxazosin is an alpha-blocker too, with the same problem.
That is a cancer operation.
An antimuscarinic is for storage symptoms and risks retention.

steps.x: **C. Finasteride.** Falls or postural drop = avoid alpha-blockers.

practice.stem: A 71 year old man has been unable to pass urine for 12 hours. He has severe suprapubic pain. He has a long history of a weak stream. A tender, distended bladder is palpable to the umbilicus. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
practice.e: Acute urinary retention needs immediate catheterisation. Tamsulosin and TURP come later.

steps.x: Initial management of an emergency: what relieves him in the next 10 minutes?

clues: unable to pass urine for 12 hours
steps.x: Painful inability to void with a palpable bladder in a man with BPH = acute urinary retention.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Drain the bladder: **catheterise**.

elim: Imaging delays the treatment he needs now.
There is no sign of infection; the problem is obstruction.
Tamsulosin may help a trial without catheter later, but will not drain him now.
TURP is elective, not the emergency step.

steps.x: **E. Urethral catheterisation.** Acute retention = catheter first.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with a 55 g prostate starts finasteride. Six months later the prostate is smaller and his PSA has fallen by about half. He notices reduced libido.
practice.q: Which is the mechanism of action of this drug?
practice.e: Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, so less DHT, a smaller gland and a halved PSA. Tamsulosin works fast without shrinking it.

steps.x: Mechanism question: a slow-acting drug that shrinks the gland and lowers PSA.
Slow onset, smaller gland and sexual side effects point to less DHT.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Finasteride **inhibits 5-alpha-reductase**, stopping testosterone becoming DHT.

elim: That is tamsulosin, which does not shrink the gland.
That is oxybutynin or tolterodine.
That is bicalutamide, an anti-androgen used in prostate cancer.
That is goserelin, used in prostate cancer.

steps.x: **D. Inhibition of 5-alpha-reductase.**

prompts.q: What is BPH, where in the prostate does it arise, and what drives it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: zone and hormone are classic one-mark facts.

points.p: Non-malignant enlargement causing bladder outlet obstruction
points.why: It is hyperplasia of stroma and epithelium, not cancer.
Cancer is peripheral zone; mixing these is a classic distractor.
A young man with LUTS needs another explanation.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: voiding symptoms (weak stream, hesitancy) point to obstruction.

points.why: BPH is the most common cause of nocturia in the notes.
Links to residual urine and infection.

prompts.q: How do DRE and PSA tell BPH from prostate cancer?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the DRE description in the stem usually gives the answer away.

points.why: A preserved median sulcus also fits BPH.

points.p: Cancer: hard, irregular, asymmetric, sulcus lost
points.why: Peripheral zone tumours are felt posteriorly.

points.p: BPH PSA normal or mildly raised; cancer markedly raised

prompts.q: What are the complications of BPH?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: split chronic from acute retention.

points.why: Residual urine is a culture medium.

prompts.q: How do chronic and acute urinary retention differ, and which drug can trigger acute retention?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pain is the discriminator.

points.p: Chronic: painless, firm smooth suprapubic mass, abdomen soft
Acute: painful, cannot void, distended bladder

points.why: Check the drug chart in post-op or vomiting stems.

prompts.q: What are the first-line investigations in a man with LUTS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the 'initial' test is the dipstick.

points.why: Infection can mimic or worsen LUTS.
Counsel about the false-positive and false-negative risk.

prompts.q: When should PSA not be measured?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two numbers, two sets of causes.

points.p: Within 48 hours of ejaculation or vigorous exercise
Within 6 weeks of UTI, prostatitis or biopsy

prompts.q: Which second-line tests assess outflow obstruction, and how is severity scored?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: residual volume and flow rate.

points.why: A big residual means incomplete emptying.
Low peak flow with a long flat curve.

prompts.q: What is the drug ladder for BPH?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: IPSS, gland size and falls history pick the rung.

points.p: IPSS ≤7: lifestyle (less caffeine, alcohol, evening fluid)
Gland >30 g or alpha-blocker unsuitable: finasteride

prompts.q: What are the side effects of tamsulosin and finasteride, and what is the definitive treatment?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: falls or postural drop means avoid alpha-blockers.

points.p: Tamsulosin: dizziness, postural hypotension, dry mouth, rhinitis
points.why: Contraindicated with falls or orthostatic hypotension.

prompts.q: How is acute urinary retention managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: drain first, investigate later.

points.why: Relieves pain and protects the kidneys.

points.p: Stop or avoid the precipitating drug

prompts.q: Why does finasteride shrink the gland but tamsulosin does not?

points.p: Tamsulosin relaxes alpha-1 smooth muscle in prostate and bladder neck
Chronic obstruction: detrusor hypertrophy then decompensation
points.why: Leads to residual urine and hydronephrosis.

glossary.BPH: Benign prostatic hyperplasia: non-cancerous growth of the prostate that narrows the urethra.
glossary.LUTS: Lower urinary tract symptoms: voiding problems (weak stream, hesitancy) and storage problems (frequency, urgency, nocturia).
glossary.nocturia: Waking at night to pass urine.
glossary.hesitancy: Delay before the urine stream starts.
glossary.transition zone: The part of the prostate surrounding the urethra, where BPH arises.
glossary.peripheral zone: The posterior outer prostate, felt on DRE, where most cancers arise.
glossary.DHT: Dihydrotestosterone: a potent androgen made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase; drives prostate growth.
glossary.5-alpha-reductase: Enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent DHT.
glossary.DRE: Digital rectal examination: feeling the prostate through the rectal wall.
glossary.median sulcus: The groove between the two prostate lobes; kept in BPH, often lost in cancer.
glossary.PSA: Prostate specific antigen: a protein from prostate cells; normal below 4 µg/L.
glossary.IPSS: International Prostate Symptom Score: a 0 to 35 questionnaire grading LUTS severity.
glossary.post-void residual: Urine left in the bladder after passing urine, measured by bladder ultrasound.
glossary.uroflowmetry: A test measuring how fast urine flows; low peak flow suggests obstruction.
glossary.bladder outlet obstruction: Blockage at the bladder neck or urethra that stops the bladder emptying.
glossary.chronic urinary retention: Slow, painless bladder distension with incomplete emptying.
glossary.acute urinary retention: Sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a distended bladder.
glossary.overflow incontinence: Dribbling leakage from an over-full bladder.
glossary.hydronephrosis: Swelling of the kidney's collecting system from back-pressure of urine.
glossary.detrusor: The smooth muscle of the bladder wall that contracts to empty it.
glossary.tamsulosin: An alpha-1 antagonist that relaxes prostate and bladder neck muscle to improve flow.
glossary.alfuzosin: An alpha-1 antagonist used like tamsulosin in BPH.
glossary.alpha-1 antagonist: Drug that blocks alpha-1 receptors, relaxing smooth muscle; first-line in BPH.
glossary.finasteride: A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that shrinks the prostate over about 6 months.
glossary.postural hypotension: A fall in blood pressure on standing, causing dizziness and falls.
glossary.antimuscarinic: Drug that blocks muscarinic receptors, calming an overactive bladder; can cause retention.
glossary.oxybutynin: An antimuscarinic for urgency and frequency.
glossary.tolterodine: An antimuscarinic for bladder storage symptoms.
glossary.cyclizine: An anticholinergic antiemetic that can precipitate acute urinary retention.
glossary.TURP: Transurethral resection of the prostate: cutting away obstructing tissue through a cystoscope.
glossary.retrograde ejaculation: Semen passing back into the bladder; the commonest complication after TURP.
glossary.catheterisation: Passing a tube into the bladder to drain urine.
glossary.prostatitis: Inflammation of the prostate, usually infective, with a tender gland and pain.
